newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Opposition stands firm on elections despite clashes.
newsitem.headline: Opposition stands firm on elections despite clashes.

text.p: After five days of protests against Bulgaria's ex-communist rulers, popular frustration over inflation running at nearly 300 percent a year boiled over into the worst political violence since the end of communism in 1989.

What began with a human chain of protest around the parliament building on Friday turned into a siege, and a battlefield when police moved in using batons and firing blank cartridges to rescue deputies trapped inside.
In a country described by giant neighbour Russia on Saturday as an "island of stability" in the troubled Balkans, government and opposition alike expressed shock at the extent of the violence.

"People who have been brought to the worst poverty in Europe and have the lowest wages in the region have the right to protest," said Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces.

On Saturday the parliament building, a Baroque-style landmark in the city centre, was filled with debris, broken glass and empty bottles. Parliament speaker Blagovest Sendov estimated damages at 500 million levs ($780,000).
A "No Stopping" sign hurled through the window lay on the floor in one office. Antique oak furniture had been smashed to make barricades and clubs.

At least 104 people were treated in hospital, among them three UDF deputies, four security guards from parliament and eight police. Former UDF prime minister Filip Dimitrov needed surgery for a head injury.

As charges and counter-charges flew over the original demonstration and the government response to it, Sofia's mayor Stefan Sofianski said he had asked the chief prosecutor to investigate who sanctioned "the cruel police assault against protesters in the early hours on Saturday".
However he also said the ease with which protesters broke through police cordons on Friday and stormed the parliament also needed investigation.
Opposition supporters continued to rally peacefully in front of the gold-domed Alexander Nevsky cathedral on Saturday, repeating their demands for early elections.
"I appeal to your reason and persistence. Nothing can stop us. We will stay here until the BSP (Socialists) agrees on early elections," UDF parliamentary leader Yordan Sokolov told the rally.

"This is the last chance for the Socialists to give up power and go away in peace. This is the last chance for our country to finally make a step towards a civilised Europe," art historian Stefan Kirov told Reuters.
"They are simply afraid of early elections because they know very well they will lose, and this time it will be forever. We want a change and we want it now," said Iliyan Iliev, a bartender.

An ominous note came from Michail Kolev, a car mechanic, saying: "The socialists should give up because if they think the worst has gone, they should better think twice. People have got nothing else to lose and I am sure that the worst is still to come." ($1=642 levs)
